'The plan read' is not used verbatim earlier, but composes two terms the deck already carries: 'the read' (chunk 4 line 36, "Aim the read at the unknown that teaches you the most", under the header 'Plan review is a high-leverage gate') and 'the plan' (used throughout chunks 2-4). rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Checked all 5 headers. 4 of 5 are claim-shaped: 'Plan review is a high-leverage gate' (line 31) and 'What you can test and check sets your complexity ceiling' (line 38) are load-bearing declaratives naming the mechanism, matching the rule's binding clause for law/consolidation slides; 'Five things a good plan has' (line 17) and 'Three pressures that make bad plans look good' (line 25) are catalogue entries naming their subject, the rule's own NOT-violation category. Closest call: chunk 1 'Ask plan mode what changed' (line 9) is grammatically imperative, not a claim — the shape rule 15 exists to keep exercise-only. The maintainer block (line 63, dated 2026-08-25, Antti-directed) documents this as deliberate: 'Header is a do-move imperative (`check_lectures §4` live-do carve-out); the prompt stays student-run (`check_lectures §6` answer-must-be-theirs carve-out...)'. check_slides §15 has no carve-out of its own naming this shape (only orientation/catalogue/phase-label), so this is an accept-note-backed judgment call rather than a clean rule match. The harm §15 exists to prevent — diluting the lecture-vs-exercise mood switch so a genuine declarative-inside-an-exercise beat stops standing out — is absent here: this is a lecture with ONE imperative header for a single, explicitly-justified live-do beat, and every other header in the file is claim-shaped. Not filed as REVISE; the accept-note pre-empts it. Blocking classification (rule added after the template's fixed partition; principle applied per the compendium's own instruction): a mismatched header grammar on one slide costs polish, not comprehension — the slide is still followable — so non-blocking, same family as rule 6.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: A bullet earns its slot or dies — three classes that read as rigour and carry nothing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Checked all 16 body bullets across chunks 1-5 against the three low-value classes. No doctrine restatement (each bullet adds a new move or example rather than re-announcing an already-landed lens — e.g. chunk 5 line 45 'Reach without calibration is what the three pressures produce' draws a NEW causal link between two previously separate ideas rather than repeating either). No self-referential design commentary (no line tells the student it is inside a pedagogy). No aphorism kicker (no bullet closes a slide by restating its own header). Closest candidate: chunk 5 line 47, 'The ceiling is not fixed. Every check you make cheap and repeatable raises it, so building a better check buys you more than approving a bigger plan.' — reads kicker-shaped (closes the deck) but the maintainer block confirms it is deliberately load-bearing new content ('The last bullet carries the raise', line 55), not a restatement of the header. Second-closest: chunk 5 line 46, 'Push reach past what you can check and you have not delegated more. You are checking less.' — introduces a genuine new distinction (delegating vs. checking) not stated earlier, so it earns its slot too. Blocking classification (rule added after the template's fixed partition; principle applied): a low-value bullet wastes attention but doesn't block comprehension, non-blocking, same family as rule 7's non-superlative sub-items.
